The Only Numbers-Matching 1970 Plymouth Sport Fury GT 440 Six-Barrel Took 27 Years To Restore
39 photos
Photo: Facebook/Brad Miles
By 1970, Detroit's horsepower fever was already colliding with steep insurance rates and shifting buyer tastes, yet Chrysler refused to blink. While rivals abandoned full-size performance, Plymouth bolted its fiercest three-twos (that’s triple two-barrels) big-block straight into a two-door C-body cruiser. The result was the 1970 Plymouth Sport Fury GT 440 Six-Barrel, an improbably sleek fuselage titan with quarter panels bigger than a starter apartment and cutthroat Mopar brawn hidden beneath its hood.
Jim Campisano, the automotive sleuth from Muscle Car Campy , spotlighted one of these unicorns at the Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals. Owned by Bill Hanzlik of Shorewood, Minnesota, the Burnt Orange hardtop sits atop the full-size Mopar hierarchy. Plymouth built 1,306 US-market Sport Fury GTs for 1970, equipping just 61 with the 440+6.
History has been very cruel to that limited batch of full-size brawlers. Fifty of them are mere memories at best, and among the eleven surviving examples, this is the sole numbers-matching car. Royalty at its finest.
The centerpiece rests under that sprawling hood: the E87 440-cubic-inch V8 fed by three two-barrel Holley carburetors. Crucially, Plymouth did not detune this 7.2-liter powerhouse for C-body duty. It matched the GTX, Road Runner, and 'Cuda spec for spec, delivering 390 horsepower at 4,700 rpm and 490 lb-ft of torque at 3,200 rpm with a 10.5:1 compression ratio. Every Six-Barrel GT paired this mill with a TorqueFlite automatic and 3.23 gears.
Photo: Facebook/Rocket Restorations Still, raw torque can only bend the laws of physics so far when hauling more than two tons of Detroit steel. When Road Test magazine put a 1970 Sport Fury GT 440+6 through its paces back in the day, the hardtop tipped the scales at 4,216 pounds and crossed the quarter mile in 16.01 seconds at 92.5 mph. The editors dubbed it a suave boulevardier rather than a pure racer with a dietary problem.
This particular example began its journey on September 4, 1969, when it was scheduled for assembly at Chrysler's Newark, Delaware plant. It was originally ordered by the owner of Doug Griffith Auto Sales, a Baltimore, Maryland Chrysler-Plymouth dealership, for his personal use, though it sold upon arrival. Carrying $752.50 in options, including $153.45 for the Six-Barrel big-block , over its $3,898 base price, the coupe stickered at $4,650.50 plus $85 destination.
Decades later, that same Maryland-delivered Mopar caught the eye of Bill Hanzlik. Already owning several four-barrel examples, Hanzlik knew how seldom a genuine Six-Barrel Sport Fury GT ever surfaced on the open market. The moment this car popped up for sale in 1999, he immediately claimed it as his own. What followed was a 27-year restoration marathon that finally wrapped up in 2026, outlasting plenty of marriages, as Campisano jokingly remarked.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Restoring an obscure C-body Plymouth is nothing like ordering catalog parts for a Camaro or Chevelle, because reproduction houses virtually ignore these cars. Hanzlik spent years chasing factory-correct hardware, occasionally purchasing entire donor cars just to salvage a single unobtainable item like an intact dash pad. The toughest treasures were the rocker moldings. Across 30 years, Hanzlik saw only four new-old-stock pieces offered, and two now sit on this car.
The tail end posed an equally delicate challenge thanks to its thin aluminum rear bumper finish panel. As Hanzlik remarked, merely looking at that trim piece cross-eyed is enough to dent it, making an undamaged survivor nearly impossible to locate. Visually, though, the payoff is extraordinary. The coupe wears FK3 Burnt Orange Metallic, a Fury-only hue applied to 145 Sport Fury GTs and often confused with FK5 Deep Burnt Orange.
Under fluorescent indoor lighting, the metallic paint shifts toward a warm creamsicle tone before deepening in natural sunlight. It pairs with a Champagne vinyl roof seen on 89 units and a matching Burnt Orange bucket-seat cabin boasting a huge console, floor shifter, and radio-delete dash found on 51 cars. Hideaway headlights, strobe stripes echoed on Rallye wheel caps, hood-mounted turn signals, and Sport Fury side-marker lenses complete the vintage spectacle.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Even that hood tells a story, sharing its stamping with every 1970 Fury, police cars included, while the A01 Light Package added recessed hood blinkers. Beneath it, the restoration obeys strict original-equipment standards rather than over-restored flash.
Every gloss-black finish, date code, component part number, and wiring harness label matches factory specs, down to the embossed trunk molding number, duplicated faithfully from reference photographs captured before disassembly ever began.
Bringing this colossal coupe back to life fell to Rick Kreuziger of Restorations by Rick in Merrillan, Wisconsin, who spent roughly 15 years pacing the job while Hanzlik hunted down prime parts. Detroit built these cruisers as 3- or 4-year throwaways rather than 50-year collectibles, leaving heavy rust along the lower quarter panels.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Because clean full panels simply do not exist, Kreuziger painstakingly hand-massaged and repaired virtually every corner himself.
Interior panels proved just as punishing, since decades of dampness warped the original backing boards beyond straightening. Kreuziger stripped the upholstery, removed the metal inserts, fabricated brand-new boards, and rebuilt each panel to look completely untouched.
Campisano likened seeing a Six-Barrel Sport Fury GT to Halley's Comet landing in your backyard, and after 27 years of relentless dedication, this 1,200-mile-ready grand tourer proves patience still beats rust and time.
